result: The simulations reproduced diverse clinical ECG phenotypes in acute and chronic post-MI, including T-wave inversion, Brugada phenocopy, QT prolongation, and upright T-waves. These ECG features were preserved across variations in ionic current conductances in population of models simulations.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this result, with one stating 'The numerical simulations are state-of-the-art' and 'The population of ventricular simulations provide mechanistic interpretation...for different types of ECG morphologies observed in post-MI patients.' Another reviewer notes 'The links of different heterogeneities due to MI remodeling to different ECG characteristics provide some useful information.' No concerns were raised about the ECG simulation findings.

result: In acute MI, T-wave inversion and Brugada phenocopy were explained by conduction abnormality and local action potential prolongation in the border zone. T-wave inversion was associated with reversed transmural repolarization gradient due to delayed activation and 57ms APD prolongation at the epicardial border zone caused by inhibition of potassium currents. Brugada phenocopy was caused by strong inhibitions of sodium, calcium, and potassium currents leading to activation failure and 29ms APD prolongation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these mechanistic findings without challenge. One reviewer states the simulations 'illustrate how different degrees of ionic remodeling can contribute to different ECG morphologies' and notes these provide 'mechanistic interpretation, down to the level of single cell ionic current remodeling.' The editor notes these are 'findings of this important work.' No concerns were raised about the acute MI mechanisms.

result: In chronic MI, upright tall T-waves highlight large repolarization dispersion between border and remote zones, which promoted ectopic propagation at fast pacing. Global QT prolongation was due to APD prolongation in the remote myocardium. T-wave duration was mainly determined by the gradient between remote and border zone repolarization times, with more severe APD prolongation in the remote zone (157ms vs 12ms difference) leading to larger T-wave duration and amplitude. Recovery of upright T-wave was due to recovery of transmural repolarization gradient caused by milder IKr inhibition in the chronic border zone.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these chronic MI findings as part of the overall mechanistic interpretation. One reviewer notes the simulations 'provide mechanistic interpretation...for different types of ECG morphologies observed in post-MI patients' and that results 'demonstrate compelling and significant evidence.' No specific concerns were raised about the chronic MI repolarization mechanisms.

result: Post-MI ejection fraction at resting heart rate was not sensitive to the extent of repolarization heterogeneity and the risk of repolarization abnormalities at fast pacing. Acute MI ionic current remodeling yielded mildly reduced LVEF (43-47%) compared with control (53%), caused by contractile dysfunction due to lowered calcium amplitude in border zone from ICaL inhibition. Chronic MI showed mild LVEF reduction unaffected by differences in repolarization gradients. Ventricles with different extents of repolarization dispersion may have similar LVEF because they have similar degrees of calcium reduction. The study concludes that proarrhythmic post-MI electrophysiological dispersions are reflected in QT and T-wave morphology biomarkers rather than in LVEF.
evaluation: This is the central finding that reviewers explicitly highlight and support. The editor states 'abnormal ECGs that are associated with higher risk of sudden cardiac death are predicted to have almost no relationship with left ventricular ejection fraction' and calls this 'important work.' One reviewer notes 'the post-MI remodeling reduced ejection fraction up to 10%...but the reduction of ejection fraction is not sensitive to remodeling of the repolarization heterogeneities.' Another states results 'demonstrate compelling and significant evidence for the need of incorporating additional risk factors for assessing post-MI patients.'

result: T-wave alternans were reproduced in chronic MI simulations at fast pacing with preserved LVEF of 49% at resting rate. Beat-to-beat ST and T-wave morphology alterations at fast pacing were due to large alternans in mid-myocardial remote zone cells. Both EAD-driven and classical calcium-driven alternans were observed, with key ionic current remodeling including enhanced CaMKII activity, slower calcium release, and suppressed SERCA pump activity. Models with inducibility of alternans at fast pacing rates presented with preserved LVEF at resting heart rates, and alternans models had larger calcium amplitude consistent with preserved LVEF.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these alternans findings as part of the mechanistic interpretation without raising concerns. One reviewer notes the simulations provide 'mechanistic interpretation, down to the level of single cell ionic current remodeling' and that results are 'compelling and significant.' The alternans findings support the main conclusion about LVEF insensitivity to arrhythmic risk, which reviewers explicitly endorse.

result: A chronic MI simulation case showed prolonged QT interval of 669ms and preserved LVEF of 49% at 75 bpm, but at 120bpm ECG reflected chaotic activity and loss of coordinated mechanical function. EADs in the remote zone generated conduction block, enabling large repolarization gradient between border and remote zones, leading to ectopic wave propagation. The key ionic current remodeling for EAD generation included inhibition of IKr and enhancement of INaL, which facilitate reactivation of ICaL. Cellular models with EADs had larger calcium amplitude suggesting preserved LVEF. The prolonged global QT interval with large T-wave duration and amplitude can be indicative of risk of large repolarization dispersion while LVEF can be preserved at rest.
evaluation: Reviewers support these EAD and ectopic propagation findings as part of the overall mechanistic framework. One reviewer states the simulations 'illustrate how different degrees of ionic remodeling can contribute to different ECG morphologies' and provide 'mechanistic interpretation.' These findings directly support the main conclusion about LVEF insensitivity, which reviewers explicitly endorse. No concerns were raised about the EAD mechanisms or ectopic propagation.

result: Sensitivity analysis showed that large changes in apex-to-base and transmural heterogeneities only altered T-wave amplitude but not its polarity and did not affect the ST-segment. Changes in mechanical parameters did not affect ECG morphology. This supports the specificity of post-MI ECG signatures to underlying ionic current remodeling.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these sensitivity analysis findings. One reviewer notes 'The numerical simulations are state-of-the-art, integrating detailed electrophysiology and mechanical contraction predictions' and accepts the mechanistic interpretations. The sensitivity analysis supports the main findings about ionic remodeling specificity, which reviewers endorse.

result: The credibility of the human electromechanical models and simulation results is supported by their consistency with experimental and clinical data from ionic dynamics to ECG and LVEF biomarkers. Diverse clinical ECG phenotypes are reproduced with different degrees of experimentally reported ionic current remodeling, and these phenotypes were consistent across physiological variabilities in ionic current conductances in the baseline electrophysiological model.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the model quality and validation. One states 'The numerical simulations are state-of-the-art, integrating detailed electrophysiology and mechanical contraction predictions' and notes 'The authors have addressed all of my previous concerns in this updated version.' Another reviewer acknowledges 'The major strength of this study is the construction of the computer modeling that simulates both electrical behavior and mechanical behavior for post-MI remodeling.'

result: The use of LVEF as the dominant biomarker in clinical risk stratifications is questioned. The authors suggest that inverted T-wave, prolonged QT in acute MI, and wide and tall T-wave in chronic MI should be considered as markers of high arrhythmic risk.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this conclusion. The editor states the findings 'are based on compelling evidence for the need of incorporating additional risk factors for assessing post-myocardial infarction patients.' One reviewer notes results 'demonstrate compelling and significant evidence for the need of incorporating additional risk factors for assessing post-MI patients.' This represents the main clinical implication that reviewers endorse.

result: A CMR-based biventricular anatomical mesh with corresponding torso geometry was used for all simulations, with an anterior scar that is 75% transmural. Scar and border zones took up 12.4% and 11.7% of ventricular volume. Various model parameters were calibrated based on literature reports, including conduction slowing in border zone, sheet active tension, and chronic passive stiffness parameters.
evaluation: One reviewer raises concerns about the model setup, stating 'The rationale (e.g., physiological or medical bases) for choosing the 3 acute MI and 2 chronic MI settings is not clear.' This suggests uncertainty about whether the specific model configurations adequately represent the clinical scenarios. However, other reviewers do not challenge the model setup, and one notes the simulations are 'state-of-the-art.'

result: LVEF reduction in clinical cases are more significant than in simulations due to factors other than ionic current remodeling: remote zone structural remodeling and elevated myocardium stiffness, and abnormalities in anatomy.
evaluation: One reviewer questions 'what novel findings or mechanistic insights that this study gained beyond the current understanding of the problem,' which may relate to the acknowledged limitations. The authors acknowledge their simulations show smaller LVEF reductions than clinical cases, but reviewers do not explicitly evaluate whether this limitation undermines the main conclusions. Other reviewers accept the findings despite this limitation.
